name: pinneapple_plugins

children.name: pinneapple_plugins.cli
children.doc:
``pinneapple plugins ...``: list, inspect, doctor, enable, disable (#1474).

    pinneapple plugins list                # every discovered plugin: name, version, source package, contract, state
    pinneapple plugins inspect openfoam    # capabilities, declared dependencies, entry point, where it came from
    pinneapple plugins doctor              # per plugin: deps present, contract compatible, executables found, config
    pinneapple plugins enable openfoam     # write to the user configuration
    pinneapple plugins disable openfoam    # write to the user configuration; does not uninstall

Exit codes, like the rest of the CLI: 0 nothing to report, 1 a plugin is broken (``doctor``/``list``), 2 a usage
error — an unknown plugin name for ``enable``/``disable``, an unreadable configuration.
children.summary: Pinneapple plugins ...: list, inspect, doctor, enable, disable (#1474).

children.name: pinneapple_plugins.contract
children.doc:
What an installed package must implement to extend PINNeAPPle, and how the version of that contract is checked.

This module is deliberately importable on its own: a third-party package depends on ``pinneapple-plugins`` (or imports
these names without importing the rest of the library) and never pulls the heavy core, the same reasoning that put
``pinneapple_stability`` in a package of its own. It uses the standard library only.

The contract
------------
A plugin is an object with four declarations and two calls::

    from pinneapple_plugins import Plugin, PluginContext

    class OpenFOAM(Plugin):
        name = "openfoam"                       # the identity of the plugin
        version = "0.3.1"                       # its own version
        contract_version = "1.0"                # the version of *this* contract it was written against
        requires = {"pinneapple": ">=0.8",      # a specifier over the installed library
                    "plugins": ["cfd-common"],  # other plugins it needs
                    "executables": ["blockMesh"],  # programs that must be on PATH
                    "python": ["numpy"],        # modules that must import
                    "config": ["case_root"]}    # keys the user must have configured
        capabilities = {"solver": ["cfd", "steady_state"], "geometry": ["stl", "step"]}
        registers = {"solver": ["openfoam_case"],   # what `initialize` adds to the registry, kind -> names
                     "model": ["komega_sst"]}       # checked against what it actually registers (#1475)
        permissions = ("read", "run")           # recorded and shown, never enforced (see #1475)

        def initialize(self, context: PluginContext) -> None:
            ...                                 # register what it provides; called once
            context.log("openfoam ready")

        def shutdown(self) -> None:
            ...                                 # release resources; safe twice, safe after a failed initialize

Registering what the plugin provides happens inside :meth:`Plugin.initialize` — ``pp.register(...)`` for a model or a
solver, ``pp.benchmark.register_method(...)`` for a benchmark. There is no second hook: one lifecycle call is what a
rule such as "a plugin that fails to initialize must not take the others down" can be written against.

Rules the loader holds itself to
--------------------------------
* **A plugin that fails to load is a record, not an exception.** ``import pinneapple`` and every other plugin keep
  working; the failure is stored with its stage, message and traceback and surfaced by ``pinneapple plugins doctor``.
* **An incompatible ``contract_version`` is refused by name**, with both versions in the message, before
  ``initialize`` runs.
* **A missing declared dependency is reported, not guessed around.**
* **What a plugin registers must be what it declared.** ``initialize`` adds entries through the registry protocol
  (``pp.register``); the loader diffs the registry around the call and refuses a plugin that registers something it
  did not declare under ``registers``, or declares something it did not register — the honest plugin written against
  last year's API that would otherwise run half its steps and look successful (#1475).
* ``shutdown()`` is called for every plugin that was initialized, including when a later plugin fails.

What loading a plugin does **not** do — no isolation, no resource limit, no enforcement of the declared permissions,
no revocation — is stated once, in :mod:`pinneapple_plugins.policy`, and printed by ``pinneapple plugins policy``.

classes.name: PluginError
classes.doc: Anything a plugin declaration or its loading refuses.

classes.name: InvalidDeclaration
classes.doc: The object a plugin entry point resolved to does not satisfy :class:`Plugin`.

classes.name: IncompatibleContract
classes.doc: The plugin was written against a contract version this library does not speak.

classes.name: MissingDependency
classes.doc: ``requires`` names something the environment does not have.

classes.name: PluginContext
classes.doc:
The read-only context handed to :meth:`Plugin.initialize`.

``paths`` are the directories a plugin may write into, ``config`` is its own section of the user configuration
(``options.<name>`` in ``~/.pinneapple/plugins.json``), ``logger`` writes to the loader's log, and
``remote_allowed`` says whether this installation may hand work to a remote executor (#1479). A plugin reads the
context; nothing here is a handle on the library's internals.

methods.name: log
methods.doc: Write one line to the loader's log (the CLI prints it, a test may collect it).

methods.name: path
methods.sig: (name: str, default: str | None = None) -> Path | None
methods.doc: One of the declared paths, or ``default`` when it is not there.

fields: logger: Callable[[str], None] = lambda line: None

classes.name: Plugin
classes.doc:
The contract. Subclass it, or provide the same attributes and two methods (duck typing is deliberate: a plugin
written for ``1.0`` should not need this class to be its base class).

methods.name: initialize
methods.doc: Register what the plugin provides. Called once; a raise is recorded and this plugin alone is affected.

methods.name: shutdown
methods.doc: Release resources. Called once, must be safe to call twice and after a failed ``initialize``.

functions.name: parse_version
functions.doc:
``"1.2.3"`` -> ``(1, 2, 3)``; ``"1.2"`` -> ``(1, 2, 0)``; ``"1"`` -> ``(1, 0, 0)``.

The contract version is a plain ``major.minor[.patch]`` number: a plugin's own version may be anything
(PEP 440 and its epochs are the package's business), but the contract version is compared here.

functions.name: contract_compatible
functions.sig: (declared: str, running: str = CONTRACT_VERSION) -> tuple[bool, str]
functions.doc:
Whether a plugin written against ``declared`` can run against ``running``, and why not when it cannot.

Same major version and a minor no newer than the running one: a plugin written against ``1.0`` runs on ``1.3``
(the additions are additive), one written against ``1.4`` does not (it may call something absent), and ``2.0``
is a different contract.

functions.name: satisfies
functions.doc:
Whether ``version`` satisfies a comma-separated specifier such as ``">=0.8,<0.9"``.

A small subset, on purpose: this package is dependency-free and only ever compares the library's own release.
``==``/``!=`` compare the release (``1.2`` equals ``1.2.0``), ``~=`` is ``>=x.y`` and ``<x+1``, and a pre-release
suffix is ignored — which is stated here rather than guessed at.

functions.name: check_declaration
functions.doc:
Validate the declarations of ``obj`` (a :class:`Plugin` instance, a subclass or a duck-typed object).

Returns the declarations as a dict; raises :class:`InvalidDeclaration` naming the first thing that is wrong,
so ``plugins doctor`` can say what to fix rather than what happened to break at import time.

children.name: pinneapple_plugins.discovery
children.doc:
Finding the plugins that are installed: the ``pinneapple.plugins`` entry-point group and nothing else.

Discovery reads distribution *metadata*, not code: walking ``importlib.metadata`` costs the import of nothing, so a
broken plugin cannot break discovery, and ``pinneapple plugins list`` can show a plugin whose module raises on import
(#1474). Importing the object is a separate, per-plugin step (:mod:`pinneapple_plugins.manager`).

The group name is part of the contract: a package declares it in its own ``pyproject.toml``::

    [project.entry-points."pinneapple.plugins"]
    openfoam = "pinneapple_openfoam:PLUGIN"

The value resolves to a :class:`pinneapple_plugins.contract.Plugin` instance, a subclass, or a zero-argument
callable that returns one.

Nothing here raises on bad metadata: a distribution whose entry points cannot be read is reported as an entry with
``error`` set, because the diagnostics command has to be able to say so.

classes.name: Entry
classes.doc:
One discovered plugin: where it comes from, without having imported it.

``loader`` is how tests hand over a plugin that is not installed (a module in ``tmp_path``, a class defined in the
test): everything downstream treats the two the same, which is the point — the loading rules are what is under
test, not setuptools.

methods.name: load
methods.doc: Resolve and import the entry point. Raises whatever the import raises — the manager records it.

methods.name: source
methods.doc: Where it came from, as ``"distribution version"`` (the docs say the same words).

fields: loader: Callable[[], Any] | None = field(default=None, compare=False, repr=False)

functions.name: discover
functions.doc:
Every installed plugin, in the deterministic order the rest of the library relies on (by name).

Two distributions declaring the same entry-point name are both kept: the second is recorded with ``error`` set
naming the first, so ``doctor`` reports a collision instead of one plugin silently winning.

children.summary: Finding the plugins that are installed: the pinneapple.plugins entry-point group and nothing else.

children.name: pinneapple_plugins.manager
children.doc:
Loading the discovered plugins, recording their state, and diagnosing them.

One object does the three things #1474 needs and #100 depends on: :class:`PluginManager` discovers (metadata only),
loads (import, contract, dependencies, configuration, ``initialize``) and answers questions about each plugin —
``records()``, ``inspect()``, ``doctor()``, ``find()``, ``enable()``/``disable()``.

The rules are the contract's (:mod:`pinneapple_plugins.contract`), applied in this order and stopped at the first
failure that can be explained:

1. the entry point resolves and the module imports;
2. ``contract_version`` is compatible with the running contract;
3. declared dependencies — the library's version, other plugins, importable modules, executables on ``PATH``;
4. required configuration keys are present;
5. ``initialize()`` succeeds (``shutdown()`` is exercised by ``doctor`` and called for every initialized plugin when
   the process ends, including when a later plugin fails).

**A failure is a record, never an exception.** Every method here returns data; the only exceptions raised are the
ones a caller asks for by name (``enable`` of a plugin that is not installed raises :class:`UnknownPlugin`).

classes.name: UnknownPlugin
classes.doc: ``enable``/``disable`` were asked about a name that no installed distribution declares.

classes.name: Match
classes.doc: One candidate of :meth:`PluginManager.find`: who, and what it said it can do.

classes.name: AmbiguousCapability
classes.doc: Two plugins declare the same capability at the same rank; the message names both, never picks one silently.

classes.name: PluginRecord
classes.doc: What is known about one plugin: identity, where it came from, its state, and the checks that got it there.

methods.name: usable
methods.doc: Whether a caller may use what this plugin provides (a broken plugin is never usable).

classes.name: ConfigSchema
classes.doc: Reads the ``disabled``/``options`` sections without rewriting them. Kept tiny on purpose.

classes.name: PluginManager
classes.sig: (*, entries: Iterable[Entry] | None = None, config: str | Path | None = None, context: PluginContext | None = None, log: Callable[[str], None] | None = None, running_version: str | None = None)
classes.doc:
Discovers, loads and diagnoses plugins. Construct once per process; :func:`pinneapple_plugins.activate` does.

``entries`` is how a caller (a test, ``doctor --from-file``) supplies the plugin list instead of the installed
distributions: everything downstream is identical, so the loading rules are what gets exercised.

methods.name: discovered
methods.doc: The installed plugins, by name, without having imported any of them.

methods.name: load_all
methods.doc:
Load every discovered plugin, recording each outcome. Idempotent unless ``force`` (which re-runs the
checks against a fresh import of the entry points' objects).

methods.name: load
methods.doc:
Load one plugin by name (loading everything else first is not required — ``requires.plugins`` is checked
against the discovered set, not against what happened to be initialized).

methods.name: inspect
methods.doc: Everything known about one plugin, including the ones that failed and the ones nothing provides.

methods.name: object
methods.doc: The initialized plugin, or ``None`` — a caller that wants to know why asks :meth:`inspect`.

methods.name: shutdown_all
methods.doc: ``shutdown()`` for every plugin that was initialized — including the ones loaded before a later failure.

methods.name: capabilities
methods.doc: Capability -> the plugins that declared it, in name order. Only what is ready is listed.

methods.name: find
methods.doc: Plugins that declare ``capability`` and every axis of ``query`` (#1473).

methods.name: find_one
methods.doc: Exactly one match, or :class:`AmbiguousCapability` naming every candidate — never a silent pick.

methods.name: doctor
methods.doc: The records to diagnose, per plugin, in name order (``name`` narrows to one and never raises).

methods.name: disable
methods.doc: Write ``name`` into the configuration's ``disabled`` list and stop using it in this process.

methods.name: enable
methods.doc: Remove ``name`` from the ``disabled`` list. It is not loaded here: the next call that loads does.

functions.name: config_path
functions.doc:
Where the enabled/disabled list lives: ``--config``, else ``$PINNEAPPLE_PLUGINS_CONFIG``, else
``~/.pinneapple/plugins.json``. A file, not a package operation: disabling is the reversible action an operator
reaches for when a plugin misbehaves in production (#1474).

functions.name: load_config
functions.doc:
Read the configuration, or an empty one when the file is absent.

A file that is there and unreadable is an error this raises: silently ignoring it would enable a plugin the
operator disabled.

functions.name: save_config
functions.sig: (path: str | Path, data: Mapping[str, Any]) -> Path
functions.doc: Write the configuration back atomically (a half-written file would enable what was disabled).

functions.name: registration_problem
functions.sig: (declared: Mapping[str, Sequence[str]], registered: Mapping[str, Sequence[str]]) -> str
functions.doc:
The refusal message when a plugin's ``registers`` and its actual registrations disagree, else ``""``.

Both directions matter, and only one of them looks like a bug at load time: a plugin that registers what it never
declared adds to the library silently, and a plugin that declares what it never registers is the plugin written
against last year's API — it loads, does half its steps, and looks successful. Nothing here is a warning: a
capability the library can find but that is not there is worse than a plugin that refuses to load.

A plugin that declares nothing at all (contract ``1.0``, written before ``registers`` existed) is compatible and is
not refused: what it registers is recorded, shown by ``doctor``, and says plainly that it was not verified — there
is no declaration to hold it to, and deriving one from what it happened to register would verify nothing.

children.name: pinneapple_plugins.policy
children.doc:
What loading a plugin checks, and what it deliberately does not provide (#1475).

A plugin is an installed package: Python code that runs in this process with the privileges of whoever imports it.
The dangerous case is not the hostile plugin — it is the honest one written against last year's API, running half its
steps and looking successful. The policy below is what the loader does about that, and what it cannot do, in the words
the CLI prints (`pinneapple plugins policy`) and the documentation quotes (`docs/core_concepts/plugins.md`); a test
holds the page to those exact sentences.

Nothing here is enforced by the operating system. The list of what is *not* provided is part of the policy, not a
disclaimer: a deployment that needs process isolation needs a process, and no amount of checking at load time
substitutes for one.

functions.name: policy_dict
functions.doc: The policy as data (``--json``, and the page's table).

functions.name: policy_text
functions.doc: The policy as the CLI prints it and the documentation quotes it, sentence for sentence.

children.summary: What loading a plugin checks, and what it deliberately does not provide (#1475).

doc:
Plugins: third-party packages that register a solver, a model, a benchmark or an adapter without a change here.

The three parts, and which issue they answer:

=================================  =================================================================================
:mod:`.contract`                   what an installed package must implement, and how its contract version is checked
:mod:`.discovery`                  finding installed plugins by the ``pinneapple.plugins`` entry-point group (#100)
:mod:`.manager`                    loading, recording and diagnosing them: list, inspect, doctor, enable, disable (#1474)
=================================  =================================================================================

    import pinneapple as pp

    pp.plugins.load()                                   # discover + initialize (pp.list_models() does this too)
    pp.plugins.names()                                  # ['openfoam', 'my-solver']
    pp.plugins.find(capability="solver", domain="cfd")  # which installed plugin can do this
    pp.plugins.inspect("openfoam")                      # state, source, contract, why it is broken
    pp.plugins.doctor()                                 # the per-plugin checks, in order

What loading a plugin does and does not guarantee is stated once, in :mod:`pinneapple_plugins.policy`, printed by
``pinneapple plugins policy`` and quoted sentence for sentence by ``docs/core_concepts/plugins.md``: the declarations
are checked (dependencies, contract version, the registrations it makes, where it came from), and there is no
isolation, no resource limit, no enforcement of the declared permissions and no revocation beyond disable or uninstall
(#1475).

``activate()`` is what the library calls the first time a registry is listed. It runs **once per process**, imports
only plugins that are enabled, and records every failure instead of raising: a broken plugin never takes down
``import pinneapple`` or another plugin. Setting ``PINNEAPPLE_PLUGINS=0`` turns discovery off for the process.

functions.name: activate
functions.sig: (*, entries: Iterable[Entry] | None = None, config: str | os.PathLike | None = None, context: PluginContext | None = None, log: Any = None, force: bool = False) -> PluginManager
functions.doc:
Discover and initialize the plugins, once per process, and return the manager.

``PINNEAPPLE_PLUGINS=0`` disables discovery for the process (an empty manager: nothing is imported and nothing is
listed). Loading never raises for a plugin's sake — every failure is in the returned records.

functions.name: active
functions.doc: The manager this process is using, if activation happened.

functions.name: deactivate
functions.doc: Shut every initialized plugin down and forget the manager (tests, and a process that is finishing).

functions.name: load
functions.doc: ``pp.plugins.load()``: activate (or return the manager already active).

functions.name: shutdown
functions.doc: ``pp.plugins.shutdown()``: ``shutdown()`` on every plugin that was initialized. Safe to call twice.

functions.name: names
functions.doc: The installed plugins, by name (no import of any of them beyond what activation already did).

functions.name: provenance
functions.doc:
The plugin set of this process, for a run's provenance (#1475): name, version, distribution and where the
entry point pointed, one dict per ready plugin.

functions.name: summary
functions.doc: How many plugins are in each state, for a one-line report.

summary: Plugins: third-party packages that register a solver, a model, a benchmark or an adapter without a change here.
